topic.title: Index laws in algebra for integer (including negative) powers
topic.subject: maths
topic.examWeightHint: M7 is two 75-minute papers of 50 marks: Paper 1 non-calculator, Paper 2 calculator, and index laws appear on both. The usual shape is a Simplify with two or three parts worth one or two marks each, sitting in the middle to late part of the paper. A one-mark part gives a single law on a bare letter (November 2025 M7 Paper 2 Q10, where (m³)⁴ and e¹⁵ ÷ e³ were a mark each). A two-mark part adds a coefficient or a second letter and is marked A2, with A1 available when the coefficient or one of the powers is right (November 2024 M7 Paper 1 Q15, November 2025 M8 Paper 1 Q11). A three-part Simplify runs one mark per part and is usually well answered: three quarters of the entry took all three in Summer 2025 M8 Paper 2 Q3. The stretch version prints two index statements and asks for two unknown powers, which is marked as a pair of simultaneous equations (Summer 2023 M7 Paper 1 Q11).

A letter written with no index has an index of 1, not 0
The bases must match before any law is used: a³ × b² does not simplify

sheet.howExamined: M7 is two 75-minute papers of 50 marks: Paper 1 non-calculator, Paper 2 calculator, and index laws appear on both. The usual shape is a Simplify with two or three parts worth one or two marks each, sitting in the middle to late part of the paper. A one-mark part gives a single law on a bare letter (November 2025 M7 Paper 2 Q10, where (m³)⁴ and e¹⁵ ÷ e³ were a mark each). A two-mark part adds a coefficient or a second letter and is marked A2, with A1 available when the coefficient or one of the powers is right (November 2024 M7 Paper 1 Q15, November 2025 M8 Paper 1 Q11). A three-part Simplify runs one mark per part and is usually well answered: three quarters of the entry took all three in Summer 2025 M8 Paper 2 Q3. The stretch version prints two index statements and asks for two unknown powers, which is marked as a pair of simultaneous equations (Summer 2023 M7 Paper 1 Q11).
traps: Multiplying the indices when the terms are multiplied, so a sixth and a second power come out as a twelfth (November 2024 M8 Paper 1 Q8)
Dividing the indices when the terms are divided — a thirtieth over a tenth given as a cube (Summer 2025 M7 Paper 2 Q9)
Adding the indices when a power is raised to a power (Summer 2025 M7 Paper 2 Q9)
Adding or subtracting the coefficients because the indices are being added or subtracted (November 2024 M7 Paper 1 Q15)
Leaving the number in front untouched when a bracket is raised to a power, or multiplying it instead of raising it (November 2025 M8 Paper 1 Q11)
Leaving a multiplication sign, or a stray plus sign, in what was supposed to be a single simplified term (November 2024 M7 Paper 1 Q15)
Writing the answer as a product rather than a power — m12 where m to the twelfth was meant (November 2025 M7 Paper 2 Q10)
Dropping the minus from a negative index, or reading a negative index as a negative number (November 2024 M8 Paper 1 Q8)
Applying a zero index to the whole term, so a coefficient disappears with the letter it was attached to

Finding the two indices and then writing them against the wrong letters, so 4 and 7 are reported as 7 and 4; check each value in the equation it came from before the answer line (Summer 2023 M7 Paper 1 Q11)

steps.decision: Split into three columns before anything else: the numbers, the first letter, the second letter. Each column is its own small sum.

twin.stem: Simplify $\dfrac{20c^{5}d^{2}}{4c^{2}d^{6}}$, giving your answer with a negative index.

items.skill: Add the indices when like terms are multiplied

options.feedback: 6 letters joined to 2 letters is 8 letters, so the indices add.
The indices were multiplied. Multiplying is the rule for a power of a power; multiplying like terms adds them.
That is the question copied out. A simplified answer is one term with one index, and a multiplication sign left standing costs the mark.

items.skill: Subtract the indices when like terms are divided

options.feedback: $24 - 6 = 18$. Each letter underneath cancels one above and the leftovers stay.
The indices were divided. This is the route the examiners reported on the hardest part of a recent indices question; a division of like terms subtracts.
The multiplying rule was used on a division. Adding belongs to a product.

items.skill: Apply an outside power to the coefficient as well as the letter

options.feedback: $3^{2} = 9$ and $4 \times 2 = 8$. Everything inside the bracket takes the power.
The letter was handled correctly and the 3 was left as it was. It is inside the bracket too, so it becomes $9$.
The coefficient is right. The indices were added instead of multiplied: $4 \times 2 = 8$.

items.skill: Use a zero index on the letter it sits on

options.feedback: $12 \div 4 = 3$ and $a^{0} = 1$, so the letter disappears and the 3 is the whole answer.
The zero index was applied to the whole term. It belongs to the $a$ only, so the 3 survives.
$a^{0}$ is 1, not 0. Anything divided by itself is 1.

items.stem: Simplify $\dfrac{20u^{3}v}{5uv^{5}}$, giving your answer with a negative index.
items.skill: Keep the sign of a negative index

options.feedback: The size of the index is right and the minus was dropped. The $v$ started underneath in greater numbers, so its index comes out negative.
Both indices are right and the numbers in front were subtracted. Coefficients divide: $20 \div 5 = 4$.

options.feedback: A negative index is the instruction to turn the letter over, so this is exactly the same number written another way.
A negative index does not make the term negative. The minus belongs in the index, where it means a reciprocal.
The minus sign has been left out altogether, so this is the reciprocal of the right answer.

findTheMistake.stem: Seán was asked to simplify $c^{24} \div c^{6}$. His working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 1 sets the division out correctly. Line 2 divides the two **indices** because the terms are being divided. The indices count letters, and cancelling pairs of letters takes them away one at a time, so the indices subtract: $24 - 6 = 18$.
findTheMistake.feedback: The set-up was right, and on a multiplication the same habit of looking at the indices would have worked. Examiners reported this exact route on the hardest part of a recent indices question, where a thirty over a ten was given as a three. A three-second check fixes it: write $c^{5} \div c^{1}$ out in letters and see that four are left, not five.

prompts.prompt: State the three index laws for the same base.
prompts.answer: $a^{m} \times a^{n} = a^{m+n}$, $a^{m} \div a^{n} = a^{m-n}$, and $(a^{m})^{n} = a^{mn}$.

prompts.prompt: What happens to the number in front when two algebraic terms are multiplied?
prompts.answer: It behaves as an ordinary number and is multiplied. Only the letters use the index laws, so the coefficients are never added just because the indices are.
$k^{n}a^{mn}$. Everything inside the bracket takes the outside power, the number included.

prompts.prompt: What does a zero index mean, and what does it act on?
prompts.answer: $a^{0} = 1$, and it acts on the letter it is written against, not on the whole term. So $7y^{0}$ is 7, not 1.

prompts.prompt: What does a negative index mean?
prompts.answer: $a^{-n} = \dfrac{1}{a^{n}}$ — it turns the letter over. It never makes the term negative.

prompts.prompt: Someone writes $c^{24} \div c^{6} = c^{4}$. What went wrong?
prompts.answer: The indices were divided. A division of like terms subtracts them, so the answer is $c^{18}$.

prompts.prompt: What does a simplified index answer have to look like on the answer line?
prompts.answer: One term, with every index written as an index. No multiplication sign, no plus sign, and $m^{12}$ rather than $m12$.

prompts.prompt: How do you simplify a fraction of two algebraic terms such as one with numbers and two letters?
prompts.answer: Split it into columns: divide the numbers as ordinary numbers, then subtract the indices of each letter separately. A letter with no index written has an index of 1.

findings.asked: Simplify a product of algebraic terms with indices.
findings.wentWrong: Multiplication signs left in the answer, a plus sign appeared, and powers were not added.
findings.rule: Multiply coefficients, add indices, write one term.

findings.wentWrong: Two thirds correct; some multiplied the indices; a few left a multiplication sign in the answer.
findings.rule: Same base multiplied: add the powers.

findings.wentWrong: Powers miscounted, such as m to the 7 or e to the 5; a product like m12 written where a power was needed.
findings.rule: Write the answer as a power, e.g. m to the 12, not m12.

findings.wentWrong: Part (c) was hardest: d to the 30 divided by d to the 10 given as d cubed.

findings.asked: Use index laws to find two unknown powers.
findings.wentWrong: Those who knew the laws found x and y (a few swapped them); most found two numbers that add to 11 and differ by 3 rather than solving simultaneous equations.
findings.rule: Equal bases means equal indices - that gives the equations.

insight.ruleToRemember: Multiply: add indices. Divide: subtract. Power of a power: multiply. Coefficients behave as numbers; the answer is a single term written with powers.
insight.aStarSignal: Turning an index identity into simultaneous equations in the unknown powers and solving them.
